claim: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway degrades mRNAs containing long 3'UTRs to perform dual roles in mRNA quality control and gene expression regulation.
source: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway degrades mRNAs containing long 3'UTRs to perform dual roles in mRNA quality control and gene expression regulation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about NMD function.

claim: Polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1) shields specific retroviral and cellular transcripts from NMD.
source: We show that the polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1) shields specific retroviral and cellular transcripts from NMD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches including decay assays, immunoprecipitation, and RNA-seq.

claim: When bound near a stop codon, PTBP1 blocks the NMD protein UPF1 from binding 3'UTRs.
source: When bound near a stop codon, PTBP1 blocks the NMD protein UPF1 from binding 3'UTRs.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments showing reduced UPF1 binding to mRNAs containing PTBP1 binding sites near stop codons.

claim: PTBP1 enrichment near stop codons correlates with 3'UTR length and resistance to NMD.
source: we use RNA-seq and transcriptome-wide analysis of PTBP1 binding sites to show that many human mRNAs are protected by PTBP1 and that PTBP1 enrichment near stop codons correlates with 3'UTR length and resistance to NMD.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and CLIP-seq analysis showing correlations between PTBP1 binding position, 3'UTR length, and NMD sensitivity.

claim: NMD is estimated to regulate 5–10% of all human genes.
source: Together, the pathway is commonly estimated to regulate 5–10% of all human genes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific consensus from the field.

claim: UPF1 is the focal point of the NMD pathway with functions in target discrimination, translational repression, RNase recruitment, and post-decay RNP remodeling.
source: The superfamily I RNA helicase UPF1 is the focal point of the NMD pathway, with characterized functions throughout the process of target discrimination, translational repression, RNase recruitment, and post-decay RNP remodeling (Czaplinski et al., 1995; Franks et al., 2010; Hogg and Goff, 2010; Isken et al., 2008; Okada-Katsuhata et al., 2012; Unterholzner and Izaurralde, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The UPF1 helicase domain forms an extensive surface for high-affinity, sequence-nonspecific RNA binding.
source: The UPF1 helicase domain forms an extensive surface for high-affinity, sequence-nonspecific RNA binding, allowing the protein to associate with the full diversity of NMD substrates (Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Fiorini et al., 2012; Hurt et al., 2013; Zund et al., 2013; Kurosaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Elongating ribosomes can disrupt UPF1's promiscuous RNA binding activity, leading to preferential UPF1 accumulation on 3'UTRs.
source: Elongating ribosomes can disrupt UPF1's promiscuous RNA binding activity, leading to preferential UPF1 accumulation on 3'UTRs (Hogg and Goff, 2010; Hurt et al., 2013; Zund et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The average 3'UTR length in human cells has evolved to exceed that necessary to induce NMD of reporter transcripts.
source: This is particularly true in human cells, in which the average 3'UTR length has evolved to exceed that necessary to induce NMD of reporter transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of natural 3'UTR lengths with experimental reporter data.

claim: The RSE is a 400-nt element located immediately downstream of the gag TC in the unspliced RSV viral RNA that robustly protects the viral RNA from UPF1-dependent decay in chicken cells.
source: The RSE is a 400-nt element located immediately downstream of the gag TC in the unspliced RSV viral RNA that robustly protects the viral RNA from UPF1-dependent decay in chicken cells (Quek and Beemon, 2014; Weil and Beemon, 2006; Weil et al., 2009; Withers and Beemon, 2010, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on the RSE.

claim: The RSE protects mRNAs from NMD in human cells.
source: We first set out to test whether the avian retrovirus-derived RSE retains its anti-NMD function in human cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays showing that transcripts containing the RSE have longer half-lives than control transcripts in human cells.

claim: Transcripts containing the RSE had a half-life of approximately 400 minutes compared to less than 120 minutes for transcripts containing the AS-RSE sequence in control siRNA-treated cells.
source: Transcripts containing the RSE were substantially more stable (half-life ~400 min) than transcripts containing the AS-RSE sequence (<120 min), confirming the protective activity of the RSE (Figure 1C, upper panel).
evidence: This is directly measured in decay assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In cells depleted of UPF1, all transcripts had half lives of greater than 240 min, indicating that the observed decay in siNT-treated cells was due to the activity of UPF1.
source: In contrast, in cells depleted of UPF1, all transcripts had half lives of greater than 240 min, indicating that the observed decay in siNT-treated cells was due to the activity of UPF1 (Figure 1C, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing decay rates in control vs UPF1-depleted cells.

claim: The RSE exhibits position-dependent activity, losing its protective function when placed in the middle or at the end of the SMG5 3'UTR.
source: Here, we confirmed that the RSE also exhibits this property when used to shield reporter transcripts in human cells, as placement of the RSE in the middle or at the end of the SMG5 3'UTR abolished its protective activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays with RSE at different positions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RSE is capable of suppressing both EJC-independent and EJC-stimulated NMD.
source: As expected, the intron-containing 3'UTR caused rapid decay of tet-regulated reporter constructs. In contrast, mRNAs containing the RSE were highly stabilized, indicating that the RSE is capable of suppressing both EJC-independent and EJC-stimulated NMD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays with intron-containing 3'UTRs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The RSE reduces UPF1 association with mRNAs in a sequence- and position-dependent manner.
source: Together, these data indicate that the RSE prevents NMD by reducing UPF1 binding to 3'UTRs in a sequence- and position-dependent manner (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments showing reduced UPF1 co-purification with RSE-containing mRNAs.

claim: A marked reduction in UPF1 association with RSE-containing RNAs was observed relative to RNAs in which the RSE was moved to the 3' end of the transcript or replaced with the SMG5-397 element.
source: As shown in Figure 2B and C, we observed a marked reduction in UPF1 association with RSE-containing RNAs relative to RNAs in which the RSE was moved to the 3' end of the transcript or replaced with the SMG5-397 element.
evidence: This is directly measured in immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The RSE retained the capacity to antagonize UPF1 binding in the absence of translation termination events.
source: Indeed, the RSE retained the capacity to antagonize UPF1 binding in the absence of translation termination events (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments in puromycin-treated cells.

claim: PTBP1 was identified as over-represented in mRNPs containing the RSE sequence compared to control mRNPs.
source: Several proteins were over-represented in mRNPs containing the RSE sequence, including polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1), heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L (hnRNP L), MATRIN 3, and splicing factor, arginine and serine-rich 14 (SFRS14; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of affinity-purified mRNPs.

claim: The RSE sequence contains as many as eleven CU-rich clusters corresponding to putative PTBP1 binding sites.
source: Indicative of the potential for robust PTBP1 binding, examination of the RSE sequence revealed as many as eleven CU-rich clusters corresponding to putative PTBP1 binding sites spread throughout the 400 nt element.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the RSE using known PTBP1 binding motifs.

claim: PTBP1 association with the RSE-ΔPTB-containing transcripts was significantly reduced compared to the wild-type RSE-containing transcripts.
source: As shown in Figures 3B and C, PTBP1 association with the RSE-ΔPTB-containing transcripts was significantly reduced compared to the wild-type RSE-containing transcripts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Transcripts containing the RSE-ΔPTB sequence displayed substantially increased UPF1 association compared to wild-type RSE.
source: Northern blots of co-purified mRNAs indicated transcripts containing the RSE-ΔPTB sequence displayed substantially increased UPF1 association (Figures 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Reintroducing six PTBP1 binding sites into the RSE-ΔPTB led to recovery of PTBP1 association to levels similar to those found in association with the wild-type RSE.
source: Reintroducing six PTBP1 binding sites into the RSE-ΔPTB led to recovery of PTBP1 association to levels similar to those found in association with the wild-type RSE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: RSE-ΔPTB-containing viral RNAs were present at much lower levels than RNAs protected by the wt RSE sequence in chicken embryonic fibroblasts.
source: In these experiments, the RSE-ΔPTB-containing viral RNAs were present at much lower levels than RNAs protected by the wt RSE sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNase protection assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Viral RNAs containing the RSE-ΔPTB+3xPTBBS sequence exhibited substantial rescue of RNA levels.
source: Viral RNAs containing the RSE-ΔPTB+3xPTBBS sequence exhibited substantial rescue due to the inclusion of artificial PTB binding sites (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNase protection assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Six PTBP1 binding sites led to almost complete restoration of RNA levels in RSV viral RNAs.
source: and six PTBP1 binding sites led to almost complete restoration of RNA levels, consistent with the effects of this RSE variant on PTBP1 and UPF1 binding (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNase protection assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Targeted mutation of the putative PTBP1 binding sites in the RSE resulted in transcript stability similar to that of mRNAs containing the inactive antisense RSE sequence.
source: In fact, targeted mutation of the putative PTBP1 binding sites in the RSE resulted in transcript stability similar to that of mRNAs containing the inactive antisense RSE sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Transcripts containing the RSE-ΔPTB+6xPTBBS variant exhibited stability comparable to transcripts containing the wt RSE.
source: Transcripts containing the RSE-ΔPTB+6xPTBBS variant (half-life >9 hr) exhibited stability comparable to transcripts containing the wt RSE, indicating that the RSE regained most or all of its function after restoration of six PTB binding sites at arbitrarily chosen sites (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Addition of three PTBP1 binding sites significantly improved transcript stability.
source: In RNA decay assays, we found that addition of three PTBP1 binding sites significantly improved transcript stability, with the distributed binding sites having a marginally stronger effect (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Transcripts containing either arrangement of six PTBP1 binding sites were highly stabilized relative to control transcripts.
source: Importantly, transcripts containing either arrangement of six PTBP1 binding sites were highly stabilized relative to control transcripts, demonstrating that PTBP1 binding is capable of recapitulating RSE function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: mRNAs in which a cluster of six PTBP1 binding sites were introduced into the SMG5 3'UTR 600 nt or 1200 nt downstream of the TC were highly unstable.
source: Consistent with the position-dependence of the full-length RSE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), mRNAs in which a cluster of six PTBP1 binding sites were introduced into the SMG5 3'UTR 600 nt or 1200 nt downstream of the TC were highly unstable (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by decay assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reporter mRNAs were comparably stabilized by co-expression with MS2-PABC1 or MS2-PTBP1, relative to co-expression with the MS2 coat protein alone.
source: Our results showed that the reporter mRNAs were comparably stabilized by co-expression with MS2-PABC1 or MS2-PTBP1, relative to co-expression with the MS2 coat protein alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tethering assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: mRNAs from 495 genes reproducibly decreased in abundance upon depletion of PTBP1 in RNA-seq analysis.
source: In biological replicates, mRNAs from 495 genes reproducibly decreased in abundance upon depletion of PTBP1, relative to their expression levels in cells treated with control siRNA (Figure 6A; see also Figure 6—source data 1)
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis comparing PTBP1-depleted cells to control cells.

claim: 188 genes were designated as 'rescued' based on reproducible increases in siPTB/siUPF1 vs siPTB alone.
source: Of the transcripts down-regulated upon PTBP1 knockdown, we designated mRNAs from 188 genes observed to reproducibly increase in siPTB/siUPF1 vs siPTB alone as 'rescued.'
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis comparing double knockdown to single PTBP1 knockdown.

claim: Concurrent knockdown of UPF1 and PTBP1 caused an increase in mRNA levels among PTBP1-dependent genes on average.
source: On average, concurrent knockdown of UPF1 and PTBP1 caused an increase in mRNA levels among PTBP1-dependent genes (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The average accumulation of PTBP1-dependent mRNAs was not altered upon UPF1 depletion alone.
source: while the average accumulation of PTBP1-dependent mRNAs was not altered upon UPF1 depletion alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: mRNAs down-regulated in PTBP1-depleted cells had a median 3'UTR length of 1577 nt, significantly longer than the median 3'UTR length among all mRNAs expressed in the RNAseq dataset (1308 nt).
source: Indeed, mRNAs down-regulated in PTBP1-depleted cells had a median 3'UTR length of 1577 nt, significantly longer than the median 3'UTR length among all mRNAs expressed in the RNAseq dataset (1308 nt; Figure 6D; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on analysis of 3'UTR lengths from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The population of mRNAs that were both significantly down-regulated by siPTBP1 treatment and rescued by co-depletion of PTBP1 and UPF1 exhibited a median 3'UTR length of 1843 nt.
source: Most importantly, the population of mRNAs that were both significantly down-regulated by siPTBP1 treatment and rescued by co-depletion of PTBP1 and UPF1 exhibited an even greater median length of 1843 nt.
evidence: This is based on analysis of 3'UTR lengths from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PTBP1 CLIP signal derived from exons was preferentially located within 200 nt of TCs.
source: In contrast, PTBP1 CLIP signal derived from exons was preferentially located within 200 nt of TCs, consistent with a role for PTBP1 in marking translation termination events.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published PTBP1 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Transcripts with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered within the first 200 nt of the TC had longer 3'UTRs than those lacking peaks near the TC.
source: In line with a role for PTBP1 in protecting potential NMD substrates, transcripts with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered within the first 200 nt of the TC had longer 3'UTRs than those lacking peaks near the TC (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of PTBP1 CLIP-seq data and 3'UTR lengths shown in Figure 7B.

claim: mRNAs with PTBP1 peak centers within 200 nt of the TC were significantly less likely to be up-regulated upon UPF1 knockdown than mRNAs without TC-proximal peaks.
source: Most importantly, mRNAs with PTBP1 peak centers within 200 nt of the TC were significantly less likely to be up-regulated upon UPF1 knockdown than mRNAs without TC-proximal peaks, indicating that this population of PTBP1-bound mRNAs is insensitive to NMD under normal conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of PTBP1 CLIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Transcripts containing PTBP1 hexamers within 50 nt of the TC were significantly less likely to be up-regulated upon UPF1 depletion than transcripts lacking putative binding sites in this interval.
source: Specifically, transcripts containing PTBP1 hexamers within 50 nt of the TC were significantly less likely to be up-regulated upon UPF1 depletion than transcripts lacking putative binding sites in this interval, while transcripts with hexamers located 50–100 from the TC showed no apparent protection from NMD (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of predicted PTBP1 binding sites and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The RSE functions through PTBP1 to inhibit NMD.
source: Through a combination of functional and biochemical assays, we have shown that the RSE functions through PTBP1 to inhibit NMD.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple experimental approaches including mutagenesis, immunoprecipitation, and decay assays.

claim: The RSE and PTBP1 effectively mask the true length of the downstream 3'UTR from UPF1, allowing the mRNA to elude surveillance.
source: In our model, the RSE and PTBP1 effectively mask the true length of the downstream 3'UTR from UPF1, allowing the mRNA to elude surveillance.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data showing reduced UPF1 binding and increased mRNA stability.

claim: The ability of PTBP1 to antagonize UPF1 binding depends on its location on the mRNA.
source: The ability of PTBP1 to antagonize UPF1 binding depends on its location on the mRNA; PTBP1 binding at the beginning of the 3'UTR causes a loss of UPF1 binding, while relocation to distal sites reduces this function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing position-dependent effects of PTBP1 binding sites on UPF1 association and mRNA stability.

claim: PTBP1 contains four RRMs, each with affinity for CU-containing sequences.
source: PTBP1 contains four RRMs, each with affinity for CU-containing sequences (Oberstrass et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous structural studies.

claim: RRM3 and RRM4 of PTBP1 are oriented back-to-back, resulting in RNA loops of 15 nt or more between sites of PTBP1 contact.
source: Of these, RRM3 and RRM4 are oriented back-to-back, resulting in RNA loops of 15 nt or more between sites of PTBP1 contact (Lamichhane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous structural studies.

claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 auto- and cross-regulate each other to favor production of PTC-containing transcripts that are efficiently degraded by NMD.
source: A series of studies has elucidated a complex regulatory network in which PTBP1 and PTBP2 auto- and cross-regulate each other to favor production of PTC-containing transcripts that are efficiently degraded by NMD (Markovtsov et al., 2000; Romanelli et al., 2000, 2005; Rahman et al., 2002; Wollerton et al., 2004; Boutz et al., 2007; Spellman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research on PTBP1/2 regulation.

claim: In most tissues, PTBP1 regulates the alternative splicing of PTBP2 to favor production of PTC-containing transcripts that are efficiently degraded by NMD.
source: In most tissues, PTBP1 regulates the alternative splicing of PTBP2 to favor production of PTC-containing transcripts that are efficiently degraded by NMD.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PTBP1/2 regulation.

claim: In the brain and testes, PTBP1 is down-regulated, allowing increased expression of PTBP2 and execution of tissue-specific splicing programs.
source: In the brain and testes, PTBP1 is down-regulated, allowing increased expression of PTBP2 and execution of tissue-specific splicing programs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about tissue-specific PTBP1/2 expression.

claim: UPF1 association with mRNAs precedes commitment to decay and does not require ongoing translation.
source: While previous studies have shown that UPF1 association with mRNAs precedes commitment to decay and does not require ongoing translation (Hogg and Goff, 2010; Hurt et al., 2013; Zund et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: UPF2 and UPF3B stimulate UPF1's ATPase and decay-promoting activities.
source: UPF2 and UPF3B stimulate UPF1's ATPase and decay-promoting activities and serve as a physical link between UPF1 and the exon junction complex (EJC), a strong activator of decay in vertebrate NMD (Chamieh et al., 2008; Le Hir et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: Interaction of UPF1 with release factors eRF1/3 at the terminating ribosome promotes phosphorylation of UPF1 by the SMG1 kinase.
source: Interaction of UPF1 with release factors eRF1/3 at the terminating ribosome promotes phosphorylation of UPF1 by the SMG1 kinase, which in turn mediates recruitment and/or activity of the SMG6 endonuclease, the SMG5/7 complex, and decapping and deadenylation factors (Jonas et al., 2013; Loh et al., 2013; Chakrabarti et al., 2014; Glavan et al., 2006; Huntzinger et al., 2008; Kashima et al., 2006; Nicholson et al., 2014; Ohnishi et al., 2003; Okada-Katsuhata et al., 2012; Eberle et al., 2009; Unterholzner and Izaurralde, 2004).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: Systematic analyses of reporter transcripts revealed a progressive UPF1-dependent decrease in mRNA half-life with increasing 3'UTR length in human cells.
source: Directly probing the relationship between 3'UTR length and NMD-sensitivity in human cells, systematic analyses of reporter transcripts revealed a progressive UPF1-dependent decrease in mRNA half-life with increasing 3'UTR length (Buhler et al., 2006; Eberle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: A large number of eukaryotic transcripts with long 3'UTRs appear to evade NMD through as-yet-unknown mechanisms.
source: these studies have been complicated by the fact that a large number of eukaryotic transcripts with long 3'UTRs appear to evade NMD through as-yet-unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations from multiple studies showing that not all long 3'UTR-containing mRNAs are degraded by NMD.

claim: Several TC-proximal human mRNA sequences capable of protecting mRNAs from NMD have been identified.
source: Indeed, several TC-proximal human mRNA sequences capable of protecting mRNAs from NMD have been identified (Toma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: Mechanisms to protect specific mRNAs from NMD are likely to be a major force shaping human gene expression.
source: Thus, mechanisms to protect specific mRNAs from NMD are likely to be a major force shaping human gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that many long 3'UTR-containing mRNAs evade NMD.

claim: Retroviral RNAs possess features that are predicted to be targeted by host cell RNA surveillance machineries, including long 3'UTRs, multiple open reading frames, and retained introns.
source: As a consequence of evolutionary pressures to maximize the coding potential of compact RNA genomes, retroviral RNAs possess features that are predicted to be targeted by host cell RNA surveillance machineries, including long 3'UTRs, multiple open reading frames, and retained introns (Bolinger and Boris-Lawrie, 2009; Withers and Beemon, 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research and knowledge about retroviral RNA structure.

claim: Some retroviruses have developed protein-based protective mechanisms against NMD to ensure RNA integrity and translation.
source: Consequently, some retroviruses have developed protein-based protective mechanisms against NMD to ensure RNA integrity and translation (Mocquet et al., 2012; Nakano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: PTBP1 has been implicated as an RNA stability factor.
source: In addition to its established role in alternative splicing, PTBP1 has been implicated as an RNA stability factor (reviewed in Romanelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citation to a review article.

claim: PTBP1 has been found to be preferentially associated with long 3'UTRs.
source: Moreover, as expected for a protein responsible for protecting specific mRNAs, PTBP1 has been found to be preferentially associated with long 3'UTRs (Gama-Carvalho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: PTBP1 binding is driven both by high-affinity heptameric or hexameric motifs and by local enrichment of pyrimidines.
source: UV cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments indicate that PTBP1 binding is driven both by high-affinity heptameric or hexameric motifs and by local enrichment of pyrimidines (Xue et al., 2009; 2013; Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous CLIP studies.

claim: Among nine genes validated by qRT-PCR as protected from NMD by PTB, eight have at least one putative PTB hexamer binding site within 150 nt of the annotated TC.
source: Among nine genes validated by qRT-PCR as protected from NMD by PTB, eight have at least one putative PTB hexamer binding site within 150 nt of the annotated TC, and six of nine have two or more hexamer binding sites in that region (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of validated genes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PTBP1 CLIP reads mapped to the 3'UTRs of each of the validated mRNAs.
source: This analysis revealed PTBP1 CLIP reads mapping to the 3'UTRs of each of the validated mRNAs listed above (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; see below for further CLIP analysis).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published PTBP1 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of aggregate binding of UPF1 to all mRNAs showed that UPF1 levels are low in coding sequences and increase downstream of TCs to reach a broad plateau throughout 3'UTRs.
source: As previously reported, analysis of aggregate binding of UPF1 to all mRNAs showed that UPF1 levels are low in coding sequences and increase downstream of TCs to reach a broad plateau throughout 3'UTRs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published UPF1 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: mRNAs with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered between 200 and 500 nt from the TC exhibited no tendency to contain longer 3'UTRs than normal.
source: As a control, mRNAs with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered between 200 and 500 nt from the TC exhibited no tendency to contain longer 3'UTRs than normal.
evidence: This is based on analysis of PTBP1 CLIP-seq data and 3'UTR lengths shown in Figure 7B.

claim: mRNAs with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered from 200 to 500 nt from the TC showed no significant trend toward protection from NMD.
source: Providing further evidence of the importance of PTBP1 binding position relative to the terminating ribosome, mRNAs with PTBP1 CLIP peaks centered from 200 to 500 nt from the TC showed no significant trend toward protection from NMD (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of PTBP1 CLIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Transcripts with hexamers located 50–100 from the TC showed no apparent protection from NMD.
source: while transcripts with hexamers located 50–100 from the TC showed no apparent protection from NMD (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of predicted PTBP1 binding sites and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Human mRNAs have evolved to avoid recognition and degradation by the NMD machinery by recruiting PTBP1 to the vicinity of TCs.
source: Together, these data suggest that human mRNAs have evolved to avoid recognition and degradation by the NMD machinery by recruiting PTBP1 to the vicinity of TCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined analysis of PTBP1 binding positions, 3'UTR lengths, and NMD sensitivity.

claim: Depletion of PTBP1 leads to induction of PTBP2 in many human cell types.
source: In many human cell types, including those used for this study, depletion of PTBP1 leads to induction of PTBP2, which compensates for a subset of PTBP1 functions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PTBP1/2 regulation.

claim: PTBP2 may also stabilize a subset of mRNAs usually protected by PTBP1.
source: As it possesses highly similar biochemical activities, PTBP2 may also stabilize a subset of mRNAs usually protected by PTBP1, meaning that the population of mRNAs identified here as protected from NMD is likely to underestimate the role of PTB paralogs in NMD inhibition.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known biochemical similarity between PTBP1 and PTBP2.

claim: Marking genuine TCs with PTBP1 is just one strategy employed by long 3'UTRs to evade NMD.
source: In addition, we expect that marking genuine TCs with PTBP1 is just one strategy employed by long 3'UTRs to evade NMD.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that not all long 3'UTR-containing mRNAs are protected by PTBP1.

claim: Yeast Pub1p was found to stabilize certain NMD targets by means that remain undefined.
source: Supporting the existence of diverse solutions to the problem, yeast Pub1p was found to stabilize certain NMD targets by means that remain undefined (Ruiz-Echevarria and Peltz, 2000)
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: Manipulation of 3'UTR structure to bring the poly-A tail in spatial proximity to the TC has been shown to stabilize reporter mRNAs.
source: and manipulation of 3'UTR structure to bring the poly-A tail in spatial proximity to the TC has been shown to stabilize reporter mRNAs (Eberle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: Long-range interactions involving multiple PTBP1 molecules bound to a single RNA may be responsible for excluding binding of splicing factors, resulting in splicing repression.
source: It has been suggested that long-range interactions involving multiple PTBP1 molcules bound to a single RNA may be responsible for excluding binding of splicing factors, resulting in splicing repression (Chou et al., 2000; Amir-Ahmady et al., 2005; Cherny et al., 2010; Lamichhane et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research on PTBP1 mechanism in splicing.

claim: PTBP1 may interact with proteins such as MATRIN 3 to promote the assembly of higher-order repressive complexes.
source: Alternatively, PTBP1 may interact with proteins such as MATRIN 3 to promote the assembly of higher-order repressive complexes (Joshi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on citation to previous research showing PTBP1-MATRIN 3 interaction.

claim: PTBP1 assembled on multiple TC-proximal CU-rich sequences could result in a zone of UPF1 exclusion, preventing the initial assembly of UPF1 into mRNPs.
source: By direct analogy to its role in splicing, PTBP1 assembled on multiple TC-proximal CU-rich sequences could thus result in a zone of UPF1 exclusion, preventing the initial assembly of UPF1 into mRNPs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data and analogy to PTBP1's role in splicing.

claim: PTBP1 may stimulate ATPase-dependent dissociation of UPF1 from the mRNP.
source: In this scenario, PTBP1 may, as has been recently described for cytoplasmic poly-A binding protein, stimulate ATPase-dependent dissociation of UPF1 from the mRNP (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to PABPC1 function.

claim: The position-dependence of PTBP1's anti-NMD activity allows stabilization in response to translation termination at the proper stop codon while preserving the ability of NMD to detect premature TCs.
source: This position-dependence has the advantage of allowing stabilization in response to translation termination at the proper stop codon while preserving the ability of NMD to detect premature TCs.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of position-dependent PTBP1 activity.

claim: A position-insensitive mechanism would prevent NMD from accurately detecting de novo nonsense mutations, reducing the scope of quality control.
source: In contrast, a position-insensitive mechanism would prevent NMD from accurately detecting de novo nonsense mutations, reducing the scope of quality control.
evidence: This is speculation about the consequences of alternative mechanisms.

claim: The population of mRNAs identified as protected from NMD is likely to underestimate the role of PTB paralogs in NMD inhibition.
source: meaning that the population of mRNAs identified here as protected from NMD is likely to underestimate the role of PTB paralogs in NMD inhibition.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known redundancy between PTBP1 and PTBP2.

claim: PTBP1 and PTBP2 may stabilize partially overlapping sets of potential NMD substrates in distinct cell types.
source: As in their roles in alternative splicing, we expect that PTBP1 and PTBP2 may stabilize partially overlapping sets of potential NMD substrates in distinct cell types (Keppetipola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to PTBP1/2 roles in splicing.

claim: With the exception of TPM1, no differences in the splicing patterns of the selected genes were observed upon PTBP1 depletion.
source: With the exception of TPM1, a known target of PTBP1 splicing regulation, we did not observe differences in the splicing patterns of the selected genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among all of the PTBP1-dependent genes, the extent of mRNA rescue upon co-depletion correlated with the reduction upon PTBP1 knockdown.
source: Among all of the PTBP1-dependent genes, the extent of mRNA rescue upon co-depletion correlated with the reduction upon PTBP1 knockdown (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: The correlation between rescue and reduction was dependent on the presence of putative high-affinity PTBP1 hexamer binding sites in the region downstream of the TC.
source: Consistent with a role for PTBP1 binding near the stop codon, this correlation was dependent on the presence of putative high-affinity PTBP1 hexamer binding sites in the region downstream of the TC (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis stratified by presence of PTBP1 binding sites shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Incomplete rescue of PTBP1-dependent mRNAs via UPF1 depletion could either be due to PTBP1 antagonizing multiple RNA decay pathways or due to insufficient UPF1 knockdown for complete abrogation of NMD activity.
source: Incomplete rescue of PTBP1-dependent mRNAs via UPF1 depletion could either be due to PTBP1 antagonizing multiple RNA decay pathways or due to insufficient UPF1 knockdown for complete abrogation of NMD activity.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for incomplete rescue.

claim: Protection of human mRNAs containing long 3'UTRs by PTBP1 is widely exploited to minimize the impact of NMD on the transcriptome.
source: Together, these data suggest that protection of human mRNAs containing long 3'UTRs by PTBP1 is widely exploited to minimize the impact of NMD on the transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq and CLIP-seq analyses showing many mRNAs with long 3'UTRs are protected by PTBP1.

claim: The SMG5 3'UTR is 1342 nt in length.
source: The SMG5 3'UTR triggers NMD as part of an extensive program of autoregulation by the NMD pathway, in a manner proposed to be due to its length (1342 nt; Huang et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2008; Yepiskoposyan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous research.

claim: The SMG5 3'UTR triggers NMD as part of an extensive program of autoregulation by the NMD pathway.
source: The SMG5 3'UTR triggers NMD as part of an extensive program of autoregulation by the NMD pathway, in a manner proposed to be due to its length (1342 nt; Huang et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2008; Yepiskoposyan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous research.

claim: PABPC1 has previously been reported to antagonize NMD when tethered to NMD-sensitive mRNAs.
source: A PABPC1-MS2 coat protein fusion was included in this assay as a positive control, as PABPC1 has previously been reported to antagonize NMD when tethered to NMD-sensitive mRNAs (Amrani et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous research.

claim: UPF1 was enriched in the control mRNP compared to the RSE-containing mRNP.
source: UPF1 was enriched in the control mRNP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), consistent with our finding that the RSE inhibits UPF1 association with the 3'UTR (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RSE contains three instances of CU-rich hexameric sequences identified as over-represented in PTB CLIP sequence tags.
source: This includes three instances of CU-rich hexameric sequences identified as over-represented in PTB CLIP sequence tags, as well as five additional clusters containing heptamers enriched in CLIP tags (Xue et al., 2009; see Materials and methods for sequences).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis using previously identified PTBP1 binding motifs.

claim: The RSE contains five additional clusters containing heptamers enriched in CLIP tags.
source: This includes three instances of CU-rich hexameric sequences identified as over-represented in PTB CLIP sequence tags, as well as five additional clusters containing heptamers enriched in CLIP tags (Xue et al., 2009; see Materials and methods for sequences).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis using previously identified PTBP1 binding motifs.

claim: The natural arrangement of the PTBP1 binding sites in the RSE may be optimal for antagonizing UPF1 binding.
source: Interestingly, although the level of UPF1 association on the transcripts containing RSE-ΔPTB+6xPTBBS is significantly reduced compared to RSE-ΔPTB, it was still higher than that of the wild-type RSE, indicating that the natural arrangement of the PTBP1 binding sites in the RSE may be optimal for antagonizing UPF1 binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of UPF1 binding to different RSE variants.
